scenarios.title: Change jobs when the puck changes teams
scenarios.objective: Update defensive responsibility after a turnover instead of continuing an attacking route.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU are navy. Gold F1 has just won the puck and now attacks the left net. The coach asks navy D1 to slow F1 while YOU find the separate gold runner F2. The turnover and assignments are given facts.
cues: D1 is asked to slow F1 while YOU locate F2.

sources.title: Hockey Canada U11 Player Pathway
sources.section: U11 Skills Matrix, printed page 22 (PDF page 22)
sources.use: Age-topic support only; no approval of these answers.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. The matrix supports tracking and basic team defence topics. The turnover and role split are authored assumptions; no recovery speed is shown. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: Which fact tells YOU that the previous attacking plan needs updating?

options.text: The right net is still visible.
D1 is wearing navy.
Gold F1 now owns the puck and attacks the left net.

questions.explanation: Possession has changed to gold, whose attack direction is toward the left net. YOU are navy and must read the resulting defensive situation.

questions.prompt: Which cues matter for YOU’s new job in this rep?

options.text: F2’s route toward the left end
D1’s ability to slow the carrier
The old plan to receive a navy attacking pass

questions.explanation: The carrier pressure and separate runner are current cues. The old attacking plan can become useful again after a regain, but it does not describe this freeze.

questions.prompt: Put this suggested turnover response in order.

options.text: Notice which team now controls the puck.
Identify the pressure teammate and the separate runner.
Recover toward the defended end while checking for a pass.

questions.explanation: Recognizing possession first prevents continuing the old route by habit. Identifying both roles helps the recovery serve the current play.

questions.prompt: Move navy YOU toward a recovery position on the left-net side of gold F2. Explain what you would watch while moving.
questions.explanation: The reference is closer to the defended left end than F2, between F2’s side and the middle. Several routes may work; the carrier, D1 and actual speed affect whether YOU can reach this relationship.

questions.prompt: Suppose D1 wins the puck back cleanly before F2 receives. What changes first?

options.text: Recognize the new navy possession and look for support space.
Continue defending F2 without checking the puck.
Continue the old attacking route without finding D1

questions.explanation: Another possession change creates another read. YOU may offer a pass or protect against pressure depending on where D1 wins it; the drill does not require one automatic outlet.

questions.prompt: Explain how the same skater can have two different jobs within a few seconds here.
questions.explanation: Before the turnover YOU could support a navy attack. After it, YOU recover against a gold runner while D1 pressures the carrier. The reason is the changed possession and assignment, not a change in jersey or permanent position.

questions.prompt: What should YOU say when D1 wins the puck?

options.text: Turnover: D1 has it; find F2 and the left-net route
The old support play continues
F2 has the puck

questions.explanation: The call names possession and the new defensive read.

questions.prompt: Which two changes define the job switch?

options.text: Gold now attacks -x
F2 is below the play
YOU was previously supporting F1

questions.explanation: Direction and the next attacker make the defensive job current; the old role is background information.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the left-net side of F2.
questions.explanation: This point moves toward the new gold attack and keeps F2 in view.

questions.prompt: F1 wins the puck back before F2 receives. Explain the next switch.
questions.explanation: Confirm F1 is now the carrier, then return to attacking support while checking D1 and F2.

scenarios.title: Forecheck with the outlet in view
scenarios.objective: Use a carrier-and-outlet read to choose an approach instead of following the puck alone.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU are navy, approaching gold D1 near the half wall in the right end. Gold D2 waits near the point on the opposite side, just inside the blue line. Gold is trying to leave this end toward the left. The coach asks for a controlled, no-contact approach.
cues: Gold D1 owns the puck near the half wall.
Gold D2 is a possible outlet near the opposite point.
YOU approach from inside the rink.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. Angling principles support considering options and body position. This authored outlet and route are illustrative; a line on the board is not a measured blocked pass. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: Which gold player is the possible outlet near the point, close to the blue line?

options.text: D1 with the puck at the half wall
D2 on the opposite side
Navy F2 in the middle

questions.explanation: D2 is at x = 8 near the right blue line and toward the opposite side. D1 is farther down the right end near the half wall.

questions.prompt: What should YOU check before accelerating at D1?

options.text: D1’s current puck position and body direction
The passing route toward D2 at the point
Where navy F2 could support the forecheck

questions.explanation: A useful approach considers the carrier’s exit options and your teammate. Looking only at D1’s jersey can miss a pass toward the point.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested forecheck read.

options.text: Locate the carrier and the likely outlet.
Choose an approach that considers the inside passing route.
Adjust as the carrier turns or moves the puck.

questions.explanation: The approach should respond to what D1 can do. This routine does not guarantee that YOU can close both the carrier and the point outlet.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example approach position between D1’s half-wall possession and D2’s point outlet.
questions.explanation: The reference approaches D1 from inside and comes near the diagonal outlet route. It is a discussion point for steering and stick positioning, not proof that the pass is blocked or that contact is appropriate.

questions.prompt: If D1 turns away from D2 and carries down toward the corner, what should YOU do with the original approach?

options.text: Skate to D2’s old location without looking.
Keep charging the exact original line.
Recheck D1’s new route and adjust while keeping support in view.

questions.explanation: The carrier’s turn changes the useful angle. Depending on speed and team support, YOU might follow under control or let a teammate take over; the original point-pass cue is no longer the only cue.

questions.prompt: How does naming “half wall” and “point” help explain this forecheck?
questions.explanation: The names identify the carrier’s space and a possible outlet space. They make the discussion clearer, but the actual positions, passing lane and changing pressure still determine which approach is useful.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call before closing D1?

options.text: D2 is the outlet near the blue line; I am reading D1's facing
D1 must pass to D2
The approach will intercept

questions.explanation: The call connects the carrier and outlet without promising an interception.

questions.prompt: Which lane checks keep this forecheck approach honest?

options.text: D1's current route
D2's outlet lane
That D1 must pass to D2

questions.explanation: Carrier direction and outlet movement change the approach; the outlet is a possibility, not a required pass.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward D1 while keeping D2 visible.
questions.explanation: This point approaches the half wall from inside and preserves the outlet scan.

questions.prompt: D1 turns away from D2. How should your approach change?
questions.explanation: Match D1's new route, keep D2 in the scan, and avoid claiming a takeaway from the static picture.

scenarios.title: Read both options on a two-on-one
scenarios.objective: Compare a carrying or shooting route with a pass using the defender and goalie cues.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. YOU carry for navy on the side of a two-on-one. Navy F2 is available across the rink. Gold D1 is inside and between the attackers and the right net. No shot or pass has happened yet.
cues: Navy has two attackers against one gold skater.
F2 is across the rink from YOU.
The goalie is in the right net.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. The manual includes two-on-one and passing/shooting topics. This freeze cannot establish a universally best play or the time required for a cross-ice pass. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: How many gold skaters, excluding the goalie, are shown defending this two-on-one?

options.text: One: D1
Two: D1 and G
None

questions.explanation: D1 is the only gold skater. G has the separate goalie role, so the scene shows two navy attackers against one defending skater and a goalie.

questions.prompt: Which cues belong in the choice between continuing and passing across to F2?

options.text: D1’s position relative to the puck and pass route
F2’s readiness and available space
The goalie’s position and the shooting lane

questions.explanation: The options depend on the defender, receiver and net. “Two-on-one” names the situation but does not make passing the correct choice in every version.

questions.prompt: Order this suggested carrier routine before choosing on the two-on-one.

options.text: Scan the defender, receiver and net.
Choose an option that fits the current lanes and pressure.
After the puck moves, look for the next support or rebound job.

questions.explanation: The routine combines the immediate decision with the next play. Rechecking can happen during the approach; it is not a requirement to pause with the puck.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example continued-carry position that keeps separation from F2. Discuss what would need to remain open.
questions.explanation: The reference keeps width and moves closer to the right net. It is only reasonable if pressure and puck control allow that continuation; it does not certify a shot, pass or safe arrival.

questions.prompt: Suppose D1 moves into YOU’s shooting line and the cross-ice route to a ready F2 becomes clear. Which option deserves a new look?

options.text: Shoot because a two-on-one must end with the carrier.
Consider the pass to F2 and then support the next play.
Wait for D1 to return to the original position.

questions.explanation: The changed shooting line and clearer receiver route make the pass worth considering. Actual pass execution, pressure and goalie movement still matter; the stated cue does not guarantee a goal.

questions.prompt: Give one cue that would favor continuing with the puck and one that would favor passing across.
questions.explanation: Continuing may fit available space and a useful shooting lane. Passing may fit a clear route and ready receiver when the defender commits toward the carrier. Explain what you would actually see rather than using “always pass” as a rule.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate in this two-on-one?

options.text: I will carry while D1 watches; show me if F2 opens
The cross-ice pass is certain
F2 must stay still

questions.explanation: The message connects D1 and F2 to the conditional carry decision.

questions.prompt: Which two events support passing across?

options.text: D1 commits to YOU
F2 has a reachable lane
The net is visible

questions.explanation: Defender commitment and receiver access create the pass read; net visibility alone does not.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a carry point that keeps F2 separated from D1.
questions.explanation: This point advances the carrier and preserves a cross-ice support line.

questions.prompt: D1 stays centred and F2 remains covered. What does the carrier re-read?
questions.explanation: Keep the puck protected and scan the available carry lane; pass only if F2 becomes reachable or D1 changes commitment.

scenarios.title: Find a job after the faceoff breaks loose
scenarios.objective: Recognize the loose puck and offer a second-play option without joining the same contest.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. The centre-ice faceoff has already happened and the puck is loose near the centre spot. The coach assigns navy C to contest it against gold C. YOU are navy and look for a useful next-pass option. These are after-faceoff positions, not legal starting positions.
cues: Navy C has the first loose-puck assignment.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. The manual supports faceoff awareness and basic team concepts. This scene does not teach faceoff legality or guarantee which centre wins possession. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: What is the puck’s current state after this faceoff?

options.text: Navy C has confirmed possession.
Gold C has confirmed possession.
It is loose between the two centres.

questions.explanation: The setup gives the puck no owner at the centre spot. A player being nearby does not establish that they control it.

questions.prompt: What should YOU watch while offering a second-play option?

options.text: Which centre actually gains control
Gold F2’s position near the support side
Only which team YOU expect to win the faceoff

questions.explanation: Actual possession determines whether YOU support an attack or recover to defend. Gold F2 may also affect the next receiving lane; an expectation is not confirmation.

questions.prompt: Arrange this suggested after-faceoff support routine.

options.text: Check the loose puck and the assigned contest.
Find a visible support lane away from the same contest.
React to the team that actually wins control.

questions.explanation: The routine keeps YOU involved without assuming the draw is already won. The useful lane can change while the two centres compete.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into an example neutral-zone support space for a possible navy win. Leave room for the centre-ice contest.
questions.explanation: The reference is outside the two centres’ immediate space and provides a diagonal option. Gold F2 is nearby, so YOU still need to read pressure; the reference is not an uncontested receiving guarantee.

questions.prompt: If gold C gains clean control instead, which update makes sense?

options.text: Turn the support read into a defensive recovery read.
Keep asking for the pass expected from a navy faceoff win
Keep treating the puck as a guaranteed navy win.

questions.explanation: The losing team’s next job depends on the new carrier and outlets. YOU should identify the immediate threat and recover with teammates rather than continue a pass request based on the expected winner.

questions.prompt: Why does “after the faceoff” still require a possession check?
questions.explanation: A faceoff can produce a loose puck or a second contest. The drop itself does not tell you which team controls the next play; support and recovery should follow the actual outcome.

questions.prompt: What should YOU say while the centres contest the puck?

options.text: I am above the play; tell me who controls before I support
Navy owns it already
Gold must win it

questions.explanation: The call respects the loose puck and asks for the possession cue.

questions.prompt: Which two updates determine your second-play route?

options.text: The centre who gains control
F2's position after the contest
The faceoff label itself

questions.explanation: The actual carrier and support position decide the route after the contest.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a support angle on the Navy side of the centre-ice contest.
questions.explanation: This point gives YOU a support angle on the Navy side of the contest while leaving both centres room; it is an example, not a fixed route.

questions.prompt: How does uncertain possession change your support call?
questions.explanation: Wait for the carrier cue, then name whether you support Navy or recover against Gold. The faceoff label alone does not set your job.

scenarios.title: Support the corner retriever from the slot side
scenarios.objective: Separate retrieval and support jobs around a loose puck in the corner.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the right net (+x); gold attacks the left net. The puck is loose in the right-end corner. The coach names navy F2 as the retriever for this rep. YOU are navy and can offer support toward the slot, the central space in front of the net. Gold D1 is between the corner area and the net.
cues: The loose puck is in the corner.
D1 is between that corner and the net.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. Basic support and individual/team play topics inform this original role split. The reference does not imply that a pass from the corner is open through D1. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: Which fact gives YOU a different first job from navy F2?

options.text: YOU have a different jersey colour.
The coach has assigned F2 to retrieve the loose corner puck.
Gold D1 has already passed to YOU.

questions.explanation: Both YOU and F2 are navy. The explicit retrieval assignment gives F2 the first puck job while YOU look for a useful support relationship.

questions.prompt: Which checks help YOU choose slot-side support instead of following F2 into the same corner?

options.text: The potential route from F2 to YOU after control
D1’s position between the corner and net
Enough separation for F2 to handle the puck

questions.explanation: Support is useful when it gives the retriever an option and avoids crowding the same space. The defender may still close the pass, so a slot-side spot must be read rather than assumed open.

questions.prompt: Order this suggested response to the assigned corner retrieval.

options.text: Recognize F2’s retrieval job.
Find a separated support position and check D1.
Offer a target if F2 gains control, then update with the next play.

questions.explanation: The routine connects role separation to actual possession. If F2 cannot gain control, YOU may need a different job instead of waiting for a pass that cannot happen.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example support spot on the slot side of F2’s corner retrieval. Explain the possible passing route.
questions.explanation: The reference moves away from the corner contest and toward the central side while staying farther out than the net-front defender. Other support heights can work; D1 and the eventual puck position determine whether a pass is available.

questions.prompt: Suppose D1 reaches the puck first and carries out of the corner. What changes for YOU?

options.text: Keep waiting for the assigned F2 pass.
Assume F2 still owns it because F2 was the retriever.
Read the gold possession and help pressure or recover with F2.

questions.explanation: An assigned task does not guarantee the outcome. A gold regain changes the play, so YOU should respond to the actual carrier and teammates rather than the planned retrieval.

questions.prompt: How can YOU help a corner retrieval without being the closest navy player to the puck?
questions.explanation: A separated receiving option can help F2 move the puck away from pressure after gaining control. Explain where the slot-side option is, how D1 affects the route, and what YOU would change if the puck stays loose or gold wins it.

questions.prompt: What should YOU tell F2 from above the corner?

options.text: I am above you; use me if the slot-side lane stays open
I will enter the same corner
The exit is certain

questions.explanation: The message offers slot-side support and keeps it conditional on the exit lane.

questions.prompt: Which two details shape the support angle?

options.text: F2's ability to see YOU
D1's route after the pickup
The loose puck guarantees a pass

questions.explanation: The carrier view and defender response determine whether the support angle remains useful.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a slot-side point between F2 and Gold's net.
questions.explanation: This point supports from the slot side between F2 and Gold's net while leaving F2 room to work; it does not decide who reaches the loose puck first.

questions.prompt: D1 wins the puck and exits. What changes for YOU?
questions.explanation: Switch to a defensive relationship with D1 or the next runner, using the left-right direction and visible support to choose.
